title: Amazon clears key water hurdle for nearly 3,000-acre data center near Houston
key_facts: The Coastal Bend Groundwater Conservation District issued groundwater permits on 8 Sep 2026 for parts of Amazon's roughly $10 billion, nearly 3,000-acre data center campus in Wharton County, outside Houston; Wharton County residents had contested them.

The permits let Amazon draw up to 78.2 million gallons over two and a half years from three wells (about 31.2 million gallons a year, enough for about 285 average US households) for restrooms, construction crews and fire protection.
Amazon says the permitted amount is a ceiling, not a forecast, and expects to use a fraction: about 5.8 million gallons a year for restrooms, sinks and offices plus 1.3 million for fire suppression.

The permits do not cover the surface water needed to cool the buildings; Amazon told the Lower Colorado River Authority it expects to need about 500 acre-feet a year, and the authority says Amazon has not yet applied for those permits.
A judge, Stephen B. Ables, recommended on 30 Jul 2026 that the permits be granted, finding residents could not establish that the wells would harm their groundwater.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has said data centers must reuse their own water, and on 21 Sep told the state environmental agency (TCEQ) to pause data center permits until audits finish; Amazon says it will comply with his water requests.

The campus would have 13 data center buildings; Amazon's Josh Weissman said each could use about 60 megawatts, up to 780 megawatts in total (enough for about 195,000 homes at peak, per the Chronicle), but Amazon declined to confirm total power needs.
Residents say they fear for their private wells, pollution from backup generators and higher electricity bills.
quote_evidence: Amazon’s plans to build a nearly 3,000-acre data center campus in Wharton County cleared a key hurdle recently when regulators approved groundwater permits needed for parts of the $10 billion project outside of Houston.
The tech company hasn’t filed an application for the permits needed to tap into those resources, said Clara Tuma, a LCRA spokesperson.
But a judge overseeing Amazon’s permit application sided with the company, ruling that local residents couldn’t establish that the wells would harm residential groundwater.
why_it_matters_hint: Water is a central flashpoint for data centers, and this permit clears one step while the larger cooling-water and power questions stay open.
notes: Permits date from 8 Sep 2026, so the underlying event is older than 2 Oct 2026; the Chronicle describes it as 'recently'. Abbott's pause on 21 Sep concerns the state environmental agency's permits, not this groundwater district's. Power use figures are Amazon's rough estimates.
